name: Dimorphism theory

lead: Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framing that faces differ between the sexes in measurable ways, and that more strongly sex-typical features are more attractive: a pronounced jaw and brow and defined cheekbones in men, softer, more youthful features in women. Users apply it to choose beards, fat loss, haircuts and sometimes procedures that sharpen masculine features.

Proponents point to hormones, especially testosterone during puberty, shaping facial bone and soft tissue, with observers reading the features as signals of health. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness exists and is mixed: preferences for masculine male faces shift with factors such as menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, relationship status and country, and some studies find little link once perceived health is accounted for.

paras: People use it as a checklist for what to emphasize: lower body fat to show jaw and cheekbones, a beard to add jaw definition, and hairstyles that frame the brow. Some look into hormonal or surgical routes, which are covered in separate entries.
The theory itself is a descriptive framework with no direct risk. Hormone use or surgery to change facial structure carry their own medical risks.

angle.text: Forum users treat masculine features such as a strong jaw and defined cheekbones as central to male attractiveness, and use the idea to choose beards, fat loss or procedures that emphasize them. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness is real but mixed.

lead: Dimorphism theory, in looksmaxxing usage, is the idea that facial and bodily differences between the sexes (sexual dimorphism) are central to perceived attractiveness, so that more strongly masculine male features and more strongly feminine female features are rated as better looking. It is a community framework rather than a single formal scientific theory, and it overlaps with academic work on facial masculinity and femininity.

Sexual dimorphism in humans is well documented in general terms: average differences in height, body mass, bone density, strength and hormone levels between adult males and females are described in the biological literature [1]. Whether and when those differences make a face more attractive is less settled. Reviews of facial attractiveness research report that preferences for masculine male faces shift with factors such as a woman's menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception use, self-rated attractiveness, relationship status and country [2]. Some studies have found little link between facial masculinity and male attractiveness once perceived health is accounted for [2].
infobox: More sex-typical facial features are more attractive

paras: In forum discussion the term is used to describe how masculine or feminine a face appears, with features such as jaw width, brow ridge, cheekbone prominence, and facial hair on one side and softer, more youthful proportions on the other. Members use it to explain ratings and to decide which features to improve.

Outside the community, the underlying subject is studied as sexual dimorphism and facial masculinity or femininity. In humans, males on average are taller and heavier than females and have denser bones, with testosterone levels roughly ten to twenty times higher in adult males [1]. The same article notes that sex differences also appear in areas such as immune function [1].

Research on how observers respond to facial masculinity is mixed. One strand reports that women in the high-estrogen follicular phase of the menstrual cycle were more likely to choose masculine faces than women who were menstruating or using hormonal contraception, and this has been interpreted under the so-called sexy son hypothesis [2]. Another strand reports that women who rate themselves as more attractive tend to prefer more masculine faces [2].

Other work cited in the same review found no association between male facial masculinity and male attractiveness among female judges, even while more feminine female faces were rated as more attractive, and one study argued that once perceived health is removed, masculinity makes little difference to male attractiveness [2]. A survey of heterosexual men in 28 countries found a preference for feminised female faces whose strength varied by country, being larger where national health indices were higher [2].

Researchers have also noted that the same genetic factors appear to influence facial masculinity in both sexes, which they suggest means any cost of masculine faces in women could offset benefits in men [2]. The review also reports differences in jaw-shape preferences, with angular male jaws favoured in Western samples [2].

Within the community, dimorphism is often treated as a core axis along which faces are judged, and it frames discussion of jaw, brow, and cheek features and of interventions intended to alter them. Reported interventions range from hormone-related approaches to facial surgery, which are covered in their own entries. Academic reviewers describe the underlying attractiveness research as inconsistent, so community statements that dimorphism universally determines attractiveness go beyond what published studies report [2].

No studies found on dimorphism theory as a looksmaxxing framework or on interventions designed on its basis. Related laboratory and survey research on facial masculinity, femininity and perceived attractiveness exists and is summarised above [2].
